how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Kitchen hood cleaning bid calculator

How much should I charge for kitchen hood cleaning?

A per-hood price treats a 10-foot canopy as the whole job. It isn't. Two kitchens can share the exact same hood length and be completely different tickets once the duct run and the fan are counted — eight feet of horizontal duct is a short add-on, thirty feet of vertical duct plus a rooftop fan through a hatch is most of the labor. Price the exhaust system, not the hood count.

Open the free hood cleaning bid calculator

What a per-hood number cannot see

Duct length and orientation. Horizontal duct and vertical duct do not clean at the same rate, and vertical runs with roof access add real time before a brush ever touches grease.

Grease load. A line that runs solid fuel or 24 hours accumulates faster than a light-cooking kitchen on the same schedule. That is a labor multiplier, not a flat surcharge.

Access and after-hours. A rooftop hatch, a cramped mechanical room, or a requirement to work after the kitchen closes all change the hours — and after-hours labor is its own line, not folded into the day rate.

A bid you can defend

  1. Price the canopy and filters by square feet, then add horizontal and vertical duct separately.
  2. Apply a grease-load multiplier and an access multiplier to the duct and fan labor.
  3. Add after-hours labor, travel, chemicals, and disposal as their own lines.
  4. Load the wage (payroll burden), then add overhead, and price = cost ÷ (1 − target margin).

The calculator does that arithmetic in your browser. It does not determine a required cleaning interval — that is an authority-having-jurisdiction and operator decision, not an NFPA 96 finding this tool can make for you.

Worked example

Two kitchens each with a 10-foot canopy: one has eight feet of horizontal duct straight to an exterior wall fan, the other has thirty feet of vertical duct and a rooftop fan reached through a hatch, on a solid-fuel line that runs light-cooking grease load into heavy. The canopy price is nearly identical. The duct and fan price is not, and the second kitchen's grease-load multiplier changes the labor again. The calculator prices the system each kitchen actually has, then rolls it into one job price and an annual contract figure.

Common questions

How do you price kitchen hood cleaning?

Price the exhaust system, not the hood count: canopy square feet and filters, plus horizontal and vertical duct, plus the fan. Apply a grease-load multiplier, an access multiplier, after-hours labor if you work after close, travel, chemicals, and disposal. Then add overhead and the margin you intend to keep.

Why do per-hood quotes lose money?

Two kitchens can share a 10-foot canopy and have completely different labor. Eight feet of horizontal duct is a short add-on. Thirty feet of vertical duct and a rooftop fan through a hatch is most of the job. A flat per-hood number cannot see that.

How often should a restaurant hood be cleaned?

Operators commonly schedule from annually on light cooking to monthly on solid-fuel or 24-hour lines. Frequency is an authority-having-jurisdiction and operator decision. This calculator does not determine a required interval.

Your costs

Common questions

How do you price kitchen hood cleaning?

Add the canopy, filters, duct, and fan as separate labor. Multiply by grease load and access, add after-hours and travel, then chemicals, disposal, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep.

Why do per-hood quotes lose money?

Two kitchens can share a 10-foot canopy and have completely different labor. A short horizontal run is a small add-on. A vertical chase and a rooftop fan through a hatch is most of the job.

How often should a restaurant hood be cleaned?

Operators commonly schedule from annually on light cooking to monthly on solid-fuel or 24-hour lines. Frequency is an operator and authority-having-jurisdiction decision. This calculator does not determine a required interval.

How much does duct and fan work add over a per-hood price?

On a default mix of a 40 sq ft canopy, six filters, 12 feet of horizontal duct, 20 feet of vertical duct, and a rooftop fan at heavy grease load, canopy and filters alone price near $495. Add the duct and fan and the same job prices near $1,982 — a $1,487 gap, because duct work is 68.6% of the production hours in this mix, not the hood.

Does grease load only change the price, or also how often the job repeats?

Both, and frequency usually matters more. Moving the same system from light to extra-heavy grease load roughly doubles the per-visit price (about $1,336 to $2,520 here), but the suggested cleaning frequency moves from once a year to monthly — 12 visits. That takes annual revenue from about $1,336 to roughly $30,237: the visit count, not the per-visit multiplier, drives most of the swing.

Why does access — rooftop versus kitchen floor — matter so much?

The access multiplier applies per component, and it can be the biggest single number in the bid. The same 20 feet of vertical duct at kitchen-floor access prices near $803 for the job; make it a ladder-and-hatch rooftop climb and the identical footage prices near $1,199 — about $396 more from access alone, before grease load or crew size are even considered.

Two different shapes: HoodCleaningDispatch is a subscription dispatch system for running a kitchen-exhaust cleaning company's call intake, night-crew scheduling, and recurring follow-up. HoodCleaningDispatch is a vertical dispatch system built specifically for commercial kitchen exhaust-cleaning companies. It offers 24/7 call intake, access-aware scheduling that books overnight work around a restaurant's kitchen-close hours, job photos, service records, access notes, and recurring follow-up so the next service date queues automatically. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. HoodCleaningDispatch's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — a dispatch platform for kitchen-exhaust cleaning companies, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for HoodCleaningDispatch appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what HoodCleaningDispatch does. It does not take calls, schedule crews, or queue follow-up visits, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. vs-tracking-it-in-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Kitchen Hood Cleaning Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. tracking it in a spreadsheet

A contractor pricing a hood-and-exhaust stop usually ends up with a spreadsheet: a canopy line, a duct-length line, a fan line, a grease-load multiplier, and a new row whenever the job needs something it did not have last time. Every formula is ordinary arithmetic. Keeping it correct as the scope changes under you is the part that gets skipped when a restaurant needs a number today.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can reproduce every line this calculator prices — canopy and filter labor, horizontal and vertical duct length, the fan, a grease-load multiplier, an access multiplier, after-hours labor, travel, chemicals, disposal, overhead, and target margin. Building it means writing a formula for each of those and remembering which ones to zero out or add back in when the next job has a longer vertical run or rooftop access this one did not.

This calculator keeps canopy, filters, duct, fan, grease load, and access on one screen, already wired to the job you are pricing. Changing the duct length or flagging rooftop access recomputes the hood-only price against the full-system price and the annual contract immediately — a field you have already hand-edited is left alone, but nothing else silently keeps yesterday's number from the last stop. A shareable bid link and a printable customer proposal with a deposit split and a price-held date are each one click, not a second document to build.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet price a hood-cleaning job instead?

Yes. Every line this calculator prices — canopy and filter labor, horizontal and vertical duct length, the fan, a grease-load multiplier, an access multiplier, after-hours labor, travel, chemicals, disposal, overhead, and target margin — is ordinary arithmetic you can put in a spreadsheet. Building it means setting up formulas for each of those and remembering to update every one of them whenever the scope changes, on a system where canopy square footage alone does not predict the cost.

What does a spreadsheet not do that this calculator does?

Show the hood-only price against the full-system price the moment you change the duct length or grease load, so a long vertical run with rooftop access is priced correctly rather than after you remember to add a row for it. It also turns the same numbers into a printable customer proposal with a deposit split and a price-held date, and a shareable bid link that reopens the exact bid for you or your crew, neither of which a formula cell produces on its own.

Is a spreadsheet ever the better choice?

Yes, when the job has a wrinkle this calculator does not model — a second exhaust system, a makeup-air unit, or a rate structure this tool's fields cannot represent. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any line item you can describe. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right fields for one hood-and-exhaust system, wired together so switching scope does not mean rebuilding the sheet.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. A share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us; your business and contact details for the printed proposal are saved locally on this device.
